extracted.intended_audience: political economists of communication, communication scholars, and media/policy researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly analysis of how framing and strategic communications ('information subsidies') shape public policy agendas and reproduce inequality, aimed at researchers and policy analysts in media and political economy. The piece evaluates mechanisms (direct/indirect subsidies, audience labor, households, capital formation) that influence policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information subsidies (definition and target)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information subsidies, like other economic subsidies, were designed to increase the consumption of some product or service by lowering its price. As gifts or discounts rather than products for sale, their ultimate target was often an elected official or a bureaucrat; lobbyists were identified as sources of direct information subsidies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two classes are defined: direct (communicated directly to elected officials, bureaucrats, or their staff) and indirect (delivered through many channels, with journalists as central intermediaries). Consider costs of designing/producing/delivering the right message to the right audience through the right media channel when assessing effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs. indirect information subsidies (efficiency/productivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect information subsidies may be more efficient or more productive of political influence than direct subsidies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the true source of a message is hidden behind a more 'trusted' source (newspaper, university expert, independent research center), audiences and policymakers apply less skepticism, increasing persuasive impact. Evaluate the degree to which source anonymity or third-party trust reduces cognitive discounting ('grain of salt').

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching frames to targets and intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all information subsidies are equally effective; many differences in productivity can be attributed to a failure to match the frames within messages with those of the targets (or with those of the intermediaries, who have well-established frames of their own).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether frames in messages align with the cognitive and normative frameworks of policymakers, intermediaries (journalists), and intended public audiences. Frame mismatch reduces policy impact (see Lakoff, 2002).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing success factors (audience receptivity intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success or failure of 'influence campaigns' depends on factors including the nature and extent of the information that subsidy providers can gather about similarities and differences in cognitive and affective receptivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaign providers' capacity to research and target cognitive/affective characteristics of audiences; such intelligence affects message productivity as processed by targets or intermediaries (Manheim, 2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging the audience: audience as labor and commodity
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences are conceptualized as labor or a commodity; audience segmentation is designed to increase the productivity of audience labor by getting them to 'watch extra' or more 'intensely.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether messages are designed for narrowcasting that matches tastes/preferences so targeted audiences can consume and integrate them into their cognitive frames, thereby increasing attention and consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience labor as investment in capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience labor should be seen as an investment in different forms of capital (economic, social, cultural, symbolic, political) that remain largely under the control of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating audience effects, consider how media use contributes to individuals' stocks of human, social, cultural, symbolic and political capital—not only as exploitation but as potential investments in capabilities and future opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capabilities approach to information access
rubrics_metrics.description: Sen’s 'capabilities' approach emphasizes opportunity distribution: access to resources and the ability of individuals to make use of those resources, including rights related to the use of information (e.g., capacity to read and understand digitally generated text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both access (infrastructure, affordability) and conversion factors (education, skills, institutional supports) that enable rights to become capabilities; consider institutional, individual, and societal factors when constructing 'capability sets' (Hobson, 2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Household as site of reproduction and information resource
rubrics_metrics.description: The household is a central site of social reproduction where information functions as an input or resource used in the production and reproduction of labor power; the home environment (books, toys, conversations) is critical to capability development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate household resources, time and money constraints (e.g., under marketization), and how these affect children's development and long-term inequality. Consider how 'pay-to-play' rules and reduced access to extracurriculars limit mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital formation distinctions (human, social, political capital)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human capital approaches overlook class and reproduction processes; social capital is closely linked to households/neighborhoods and civic engagement; political capital is symbolic capital used to exercise power and influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish among types of capital when assessing interventions: human capital (education/skills), social capital (networks, civic engagement; depleted by non-use), and political capital (organizational accumulation, negotiation with stakeholders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political participation and policy influence (limits of engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increases in participation requirements and digital communication ease interactions with officials, but higher engagement in some groups may not translate into policy-relevant goals; economic elites have disproportionate policy impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether increased access/engagement yields measurable policy influence. Consider empirical findings (e.g., Gilens & Page) showing near-zero average-citizen influence once elites/interest groups are controlled for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion surveys as intermediaries and biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion surveys—often developed by news organizations or financed by information-intensive corporations—can reflect self-interested framing and be reported in the press or cited in congressional testimony, thereby redistributing frames to policymakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize survey sponsorship, question framing, and the pipeline by which survey results reach policymakers; corporate-funded surveys may understate privacy concerns or otherwise present biased impressions of public willingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketization, audience segmentation, and increased targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketization and increases in media channels enabled audience segmentation and targeting by marketing and public relations sectors, allowing strategically framed persuasive messages to be directed at particular segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging strategic communications, assess the degree of segmentation, targeting precision, and whether background content/frame matching facilitates consumption without demanding interpretive labor from audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic constraints and dependence on well-crafted subsidies
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in the news business (emphasis on audience attention, engagement, value) have increased journalists' dependence on well-crafted information subsidies; journalists have less time to do original research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine news production conditions: time pressures, metrics of audience attention, use of PR materials, bloggers ('media catching'), and expert-request services. These conditions affect what information reaches policymakers and the public.
